svg.title: Google Flu Trends: a connection that passed its first test, then drifted
svg.desc: How the 2008 model was built, a 2003 to 2014 timeline of changes to search, a 108-week waffle of overestimates, and mean absolute errors for three models.
svg.text: LIA / PART III / III-12 CONNECTIONS THAT FAILED
Google Flu Trends: a connection that passed its first test, then drifted with its
The model assumed a fixed relation between the share of certain queries and the level of illness. The service that produced the
queries did not hold that relation fixed.

Green bar, 21 August 2011 to 1 September 2013: estimates too high in 100 of 108 weeks.
The 2011 to 2012 season was overshot by more than 50 percent.
green: too high; open: not; cells are not in week order
lagged CDC data only, two or three weeks old
Fifty million candidate terms were matched against 1,152 data points; queries about high school basketball scored well
because the seasons coincide. The 45 queries were never published, so the analysis could not be replicated from outside.
Sources: Ginsberg et al., Detecting influenza epidemics using search engine query data, Nature 457, published online November 2008; Lazer,
Kennedy, King and Vespignani 2014, The Parable of Google Flu, Science. Bars start at zero.
